beats.text: An engineer pushes a commit, which sends it to the team's shared server. Then they notice a typo in the message, fix it with git commit --amend, and push again. The push is rejected. Git prints a hint: use git pull before pushing again.
beats.tele: An engineer pushes a commit, which sends it to the team's shared server. Then they notice a typo in the message, fix it with `git commit --amend`, and push again. The push is rejected. Git prints a hint: use `git pull` before pushing again.

beats.text: They pull, which fetches the server's commits and merges them in. Now the history has the old commit, the new commit, and a merge of the two: two versions of one change, joined together, on a shared branch. Was pulling the right move? Say yes or no.
beats.tele: They pull, which fetches the server's commits and merges them in. Now the history has the old commit, the new commit, and a merge of the two: two versions of one change, joined together, on a shared branch. Was pulling the right move? Say yes or no.

beats.text: No. The hint was the wrong advice for this situation, and following it made things worse. To see why, you need one fact: amend doesn't edit a commit. It creates a sibling, and moves your branch to it. Today is about that fact, and about what makes a commit good enough that you rarely need to amend it. And you'll leave with the two right moves for that engineer.

beats.text: Amend. In one sentence: git commit --amend writes a new commit that takes the place of the current one: same parent, new tree and message as you choose, new ID. It is 🟡 CAUTION.
beats.tele: Amend. In one sentence: `git commit --amend` writes a new commit that takes the place of the current one: same parent, new tree and message as you choose, new ID. It is 🟡 CAUTION.

beats.text: Quick quiz, three options. What happens to the old commit: is it edited, deleted, or left where it was? Say your answer.
beats.tele: Quick quiz, three options. What happens to the old commit: is it edited, deleted, or left where it was? Say your answer.

beats.text: Left where it was. The manual's description is "Replace the tip of the current branch by creating a new commit", and "The new commit has the same parents and author as the current one". The old commit is neither modified nor deleted. The branch stops pointing at it, and only reflog entries still refer to it. The reflog is Git's local journal of where a branch has pointed.
beats.tele: Left where it was. The manual's description is "Replace the tip of the current branch by creating a new commit", and "The new commit has the same parents and author as the current one". The old commit is neither modified nor deleted. The branch stops pointing at it, and only reflog entries still refer to it. The reflog is Git's local journal of where a branch has pointed.

beats.text: How long the old commit survives. By default, a reflog entry that is not reachable from the current tip expires after 30 days, and any other entry after 90. An object that no ref and no reflog entry refers to is pruned by maintenance once it is more than two weeks old. A ref is a name for a commit, such as a branch. The lab configuration sets the two reflog values to never, so replays don't depend on the calendar.

The lab configuration sets the two reflog values to `never`, so replays don't depend on the calendar.

beats.text: When to amend, and when not. Amend freely while a commit exists only in your repository. --no-edit keeps the message, --only leaves staged changes out, and --reset-author repairs a wrong identity. Remember that everything staged goes into an amend unless you say --only.

beats.text: Don't amend what others may have: on a shared branch an amend produces a divergence for every colleague. And an amend doesn't delete anything: a secret committed and then amended away is still in the old commit, in your reflog, and on the server if it was pushed. Rotate the secret.

beats.text: Empty commits. An empty commit has the same tree as its parent: a point in history with a message and no change. Without --allow-empty, Git refuses. The manual says the option "is primarily for use by foreign SCM interface scripts". Teams use it to start a push-triggered pipeline, an automated build, without touching a file. Two cautions from the textbook. A pipeline filtered by changed paths has no path to match, so an empty commit may not start it. And the commit stays in history. Empty commits are permanent.

beats.text: Trailers. In one sentence: a trailer is a Key: value line in the last paragraph of a commit message: ordinary text, placed where Git and other tools can find and parse it. git commit -s adds a Signed-off-by trailer with the committer's identity, and --trailer adds any other. The trailers are part of the message, so they are part of the commit object and of its ID.
beats.tele: Trailers. In one sentence: a trailer is a `Key: value` line in the last paragraph of a commit message: ordinary text, placed where Git and other tools can find and parse it. `git commit -s` adds a `Signed-off-by` trailer with the committer's identity, and `--trailer` adds any other. The trailers are part of the message, so they are part of the commit object and of its ID.

beats.text: The rules. Git recognises a trailer block only at the end of the message, after an empty line. Every line of the block must be a trailer, unless at least a quarter of the lines are, and one of them has a key that Git generates itself, such as Signed-off-by, or a key defined in your configuration.
beats.tele: The rules. Git recognises a trailer block only at the end of the message, after an empty line. Every line of the block must be a trailer, unless at least a quarter of the lines are, and one of them has a key that Git generates itself, such as `Signed-off-by`, or a key defined in your configuration.

beats.text: What they mean. Signed-off-by: a statement defined by the project, commonly the Developer Certificate of Origin. It's text, not a cryptographic signature. Co-authored-by: credit for a further author. Git only stores the line. Others such as Reviewed-by, Refs and Fixes mean whatever your team defines.
beats.tele: What they mean. `Signed-off-by`: a statement defined by the project, commonly the Developer Certificate of Origin. It's text, not a cryptographic signature. `Co-authored-by`: credit for a further author. Git only stores the line. Others such as `Reviewed-by`, `Refs` and `Fixes` mean whatever your team defines.

beats.text: Version notes from the textbook. git commit --trailer exists since Git 2.32. git shortlog --group=trailer:<key> since Git 2.29. And up to Git 2.55 the trailer parser can take a line that begins with a URL for a trailer. Git 2.56 no longer does. That last one is "added in Git 2.56, not run here".

beats.text: How Git reads a message. Two rules matter. First, the title is the text up to the first empty line, not the first line. Without the empty line, your body becomes part of the title. Second, when a message passes through the editor, lines that begin with # are comments and are removed. Don't start a line with #.

beats.text: Atomic commits. An atomic commit contains one logical change, complete enough that the project still builds and passes its tests. The Git project's rule: "Make separate commits for logically separate changes". The test of a good split is what a revert would do. git revert is 🟡 CAUTION: it adds one commit that applies the inverse change. In the picture from today's demo, that's the third commit, undoing the second.

beats.text: Signatures. A signed commit carries its signature inside the commit object, in a gpgsig header between the committer line and the message. Because it's inside the object, it's covered by the commit ID, and signing a commit that already exists means writing a new commit. Don't confuse the two options: capital -S signs with a key, and small -s adds the Signed-off-by text.

beats.text: For amend, forget the word "edit". Picture a fork with two short prongs. Both prongs grow from the same parent. One is the commit you made first. The other is the commit amend made. The branch label is moved from the first prong to the second. Nothing is erased.

beats.text: Now read the hook with that picture. The server holds the first prong. You hold the second. Your branch is one commit ahead and one commit behind at the same time. A pull merges the prongs. That's why the hint is wrong here.

beats.text: The model's limit: the first prong is not permanent. It's kept by reflog entries, and those expire. So "nothing is erased" is true today and has a time limit.

beats.text: A commit with a typo in its message, and a forgotten test file. git commit --amend 🟡 CAUTION. Predict: after the amend, how many commits does git log show, two or three, and what is the ID of the tip? Say it out loud.

beats.text: Still two commits. The log shows 8f6fa22 where 831f9ff was. The Date: line in the summary is the author date, carried over by the amend. Where is 831f9ff now? Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: In the reflog, one entry down. git cat-file -p 'HEAD@{1}' prints the old object: same parent, same author line, and a different tree, committer time and message. Two commits that share a parent.

beats.text: No branch contains the old commit, and git log --all doesn't list it. git fsck --no-reflogs reports it as dangling: only the reflog still refers to it.

beats.text: git push 🟡 CAUTION is rejected as a non-fast-forward, and the hint says to pull. Don't follow the hint: it would merge two versions of one commit. Here are the two right moves I promised, from the textbook. If others may have the published commit, return to it with git reset --soft '@{u}', which is 🟡 CAUTION, and fix the mistake in a new commit. If the branch is yours alone, replace the published commit deliberately. That's a topic of Part 2.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: git push rejected after an amend, then a pull. Root cause: the amend created a sibling of the published commit; the pull merges two versions of one commit.
beats.tele: `git push` rejected after an amend, then a pull. Root cause: the amend created a sibling of the published commit; the pull merges two versions of one commit.

beats.text: An amend swallowed unrelated staged changes. Root cause: everything staged goes into an amend unless you say --only; run git status before amending.
beats.tele: An amend swallowed unrelated staged changes. Root cause: everything staged goes into an amend unless you say `--only`; run `git status` before amending.

beats.text: A line of the message is missing. Root cause: the line began with # and the message went through the editor, where such lines are comments.
beats.tele: A line of the message is missing. Root cause: the line began with `#` and the message went through the editor, where such lines are comments.

beats.text: git log --oneline shows a very long title. Root cause: there is no empty line after the first line, and the title is the text up to the first empty line.

beats.text: A trailer is not found by tooling. Root cause: it is not in the last paragraph, or a sentence shares its block; add trailers with --trailer, not by hand.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. An evaluation team puts the ticket number and the evaluation-run ID of each change into trailers. The textbook's reason: a ticket number or a run ID in a trailer travels with the commit into every clone, and a pull-request label doesn't. A year later, "which commits belong to this ticket?" is one git log format away, on any machine, with no network.

beats.text: A trailer is a Key: value line in the last paragraph of the message, and Git parses it only if the block follows the rules. The title is everything up to the first empty line, and tools use it everywhere. An atomic commit is one logical change that can be reverted alone. A signature lives in a gpgsig header inside the commit object.
